question: When two power-driven vessels are approaching each other head-on, what should each operator do?
choice_a: Each should alter course to port (left) so the vessels pass starboard side to starboard side
choice_b: Neither vessel should change course; the faster vessel has right-of-way
choice_c: Each should alter course to starboard (right) so the vessels pass port side to port side
choice_d: Both vessels should stop dead in the water and wait for instructions
explanation: In a head-on meeting situation, the Navigation Rules direct both power-driven vessels to alter course to starboard, passing each other port-to-port, similar to cars driving on the right.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules (33 CFR) -- head-on meeting situation, as taught in TPWD boater education

question: In a crossing situation between two power-driven vessels, which vessel is the 'give-way' vessel required to take early and substantial action to avoid collision?
choice_a: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching from its own port (left) side
choice_d: The vessel that has the other vessel approaching from its own starboard (right) side
explanation: When two power-driven vessels are crossing, the vessel that sees the other on its own starboard side is the give-way vessel and must yield; the other is the stand-on vessel and should maintain course and speed.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- crossing situation right-of-way

question: In an overtaking situation, which vessel must give way?
choice_a: The overtaking vessel (the one coming from behind) must keep clear of the vessel being overtaken until it is safely past
choice_b: The vessel being overtaken must always move out of the way
choice_c: Neither vessel has an obligation in an overtaking situation
choice_d: The overtaking vessel automatically has the right-of-way
explanation: The vessel doing the overtaking is always the give-way vessel and must keep clear of the vessel being passed, regardless of whether the vessels are under sail or power.

question: As a general rule, when a sailboat under sail alone meets a motorboat, which vessel has right-of-way?
choice_a: The motorboat always has right-of-way over sailboats
choice_b: The sailboat, because a vessel under sail generally has right-of-way over a power-driven vessel
choice_c: Right-of-way depends only on which vessel is larger
choice_d: Right-of-way always goes to whichever vessel arrived at the area first
explanation: A sailing vessel operating under sail alone (not under engine power) generally has right-of-way over a power-driven vessel, though a sailboat under engine power is legally considered a power-driven vessel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- sail vs. power right-of-way

question: Along the general order of vessel priority recognized in the Navigation Rules, which type of vessel generally ranks at or near the top, meaning most other vessels must stay out of its way?
choice_a: A personal watercraft engaged in recreational riding
choice_b: A small fishing boat trolling near shore
choice_c: A vessel restricted in its ability to maneuver, such as one engaged in dredging or laying cable
choice_d: Any vessel simply because it is the largest one present
explanation: The general priority order gives higher standing to vessels not under command, vessels restricted in their ability to maneuver (such as those laying cable or dredging), and vessels engaged in commercial fishing, above ordinary power-driven recreational vessels.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- general priority of vessels

question: What action should the 'stand-on' vessel take in a crossing or meeting situation where it has right-of-way?
choice_a: Immediately speed up to get out of the way
choice_b: Turn sharply toward the other vessel to signal right-of-way
choice_c: Stop the engine completely at all times
choice_d: Maintain its current course and speed so the give-way vessel can predict its movement, while remaining ready to take action if a collision becomes imminent
explanation: The stand-on vessel should hold its course and speed so the give-way vessel can reliably predict its movement, but it must still act to avoid a collision if the give-way vessel fails to yield in time.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- stand-on vessel obligations

question: What does one short blast of a horn mean when signaling intentions to a nearby vessel under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: I intend to alter my course to starboard (turn right)
choice_b: I intend to alter my course to port (turn left)
choice_c: I am operating astern propulsion (backing up)
choice_d: I am in distress and require immediate assistance
explanation: Under the maneuvering and warning signal rules, one short blast signals an intent to turn to starboard; two short blasts signal an intent to turn to port; three short blasts signal operating astern propulsion.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- sound signals for maneuvering

question: What do five or more short, rapid blasts of a horn mean between vessels?
choice_a: A friendly greeting between passing boaters
choice_b: A danger or doubt signal, warning that the other vessel's intentions or actions are not understood or are considered unsafe
choice_c: A signal that a vessel is anchoring for the night
choice_d: A signal used only to celebrate finishing a race
explanation: Five or more short, rapid blasts is the danger/doubt signal, alerting another vessel that its intentions are unclear or that a collision risk exists.

question: Why must every vessel maintain a proper lookout at all times by sight and hearing?
choice_a: It is only a suggestion, not a legal requirement
choice_b: It applies only to vessels longer than 65 feet
choice_c: To make a full appraisal of the situation and the risk of collision, as required by the Navigation Rules
choice_d: It is required only during nighttime hours
explanation: The Navigation Rules require every vessel to maintain a proper lookout by sight and hearing at all times, appropriate to the conditions, to properly assess the risk of collision.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- lookout requirement, Rule 5

question: What does 'safe speed' mean under the Navigation Rules?
choice_a: The fastest speed the vessel's engine is capable of
choice_b: A single fixed speed that applies identically on every body of water
choice_c: Any speed as long as no other boats are visible at that moment
choice_d: A speed at which a vessel can take proper and effective action to avoid collision, adjusted for visibility, traffic density, and maneuverability -- not simply the posted speed limit
explanation: Safe speed is a judgment based on conditions such as visibility, traffic, and the vessel's stopping ability -- not a fixed number -- so a boat can still exceed a safe speed even if under a posted numeric limit.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- safe speed, Rule 6

question: In narrow channels, which vessels does the Navigation Rules direct to stay to the outer edge of the channel and, when practicable, avoid impeding the passage of larger vessels that can only navigate safely within the channel?
choice_a: Vessels less than 20 meters, sailing vessels, and vessels engaged in fishing
choice_c: Only vessels over 65 feet in length
choice_d: No vessel type receives special treatment in a narrow channel
explanation: The narrow channel rule requires small vessels under 20 meters, sailing vessels, and fishing vessels to avoid impeding the passage of a larger vessel that can only navigate safely within a narrow channel.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- narrow channel rule, Rule 9

question: What should a boat operator generally do when approaching a vessel that is anchored, disabled, or otherwise not under command?
choice_a: Pass as close as possible to save time
choice_b: Keep well clear and give it a wide berth, since it may be unable to maneuver to avoid a collision
choice_c: Sound the danger signal and proceed at full speed
choice_d: Assume it always has to give way regardless of its situation
explanation: A vessel not under command or otherwise unable to maneuver cannot reliably take avoiding action, so other vessels must keep well clear and pass at a safe distance.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules -- vessels restricted in ability to maneuver

question: On Texas lakes and rivers, what right-of-way principle generally applies between a vessel operating on the main body of a lake and a vessel leaving a dock, cove, or marina?
choice_a: The departing vessel always has right-of-way over vessels already on open water
choice_b: Whichever vessel honks first automatically gets the right-of-way
choice_c: The vessel already operating on the open water generally has the right-of-way over a vessel just getting underway from a dock or cove
choice_d: There is no right-of-way consideration when leaving a dock
explanation: A boat getting underway from a dock, cove, or restricted area should yield to vessels already navigating in open water, since the departing operator has a clearer view of oncoming traffic.
source_note: TPWD Boater Education Manual -- right-of-way near docks and marinas

question: How do the Navigation Rules treat a personal watercraft (PWC) in a right-of-way situation with another vessel?
choice_a: PWCs are exempt from all navigation right-of-way rules
choice_b: A PWC always has right-of-way over larger vessels
choice_c: A PWC only needs to follow right-of-way rules when towing a skier
choice_d: A PWC is a power-driven vessel and must follow the same crossing, meeting, and overtaking right-of-way rules as any other power-driven vessel
explanation: A PWC is legally a power-driven vessel and is bound by the same meeting, crossing, and overtaking right-of-way rules that apply to any other motorboat.
source_note: Inland Navigation Rules / TPWD PWC operation rules
